questions.q: When you run `docker run hello-world` and the image isn't present locally, what happens first?
options: Docker refuses to run and shows an error
Docker pulls the image from Docker Hub, the default public registry
Docker builds the image from source code automatically
Docker asks you to manually download the image file
questions.explain: If an image isn't already cached locally, `docker run` automatically pulls it from Docker Hub before creating and starting a container from it.

questions.q: What do the `-i` and `-t` flags do when combined in `docker run -it ubuntu bash`?
options: They install Docker and start the daemon
They keep STDIN open and allocate a terminal, together producing a usable interactive shell
They limit the container's CPU and memory usage
They tell Docker to run the container in the background
questions.explain: `-i` (interactive) keeps standard input open, and `-t` (tty) allocates a terminal -- combined, they let you type and see output like a normal shell session.

questions.q: What is the relationship between an image and a container?
options: They are the same thing, just different names for it
An image is a read-only template; a container is a running (or stopped) instance created from that image
A container is the template, and an image is created from it
An image can only ever produce one container
questions.explain: The image is the unchanging template. Each `docker run` creates a new container -- a live instance -- from that same image, and you can create many containers from one image.

questions.q: Why does a container started with `docker run -it ubuntu bash` stop as soon as you type `exit`?
options: Because Docker automatically deletes all containers after 60 seconds
Because the container's only running process was that bash shell, and the container stops when its main process ends
Because exit is a special Docker command that shuts down the whole daemon
Because Ubuntu images are not allowed to run for more than one command
questions.explain: A container keeps running only as long as its main process is running. Since bash was that process, exiting the shell ends the container.

questions.q: Which command lists every container on the host, including ones that have already stopped?
options: docker images
docker run hello-world
docker ps -a
docker exit --all
questions.explain: `docker ps` alone only shows running containers; adding `-a` lists every container regardless of its current state, running or stopped.
